guide.title: Chapter 7 Fractions Study Guide
guide.intro: Original Study Scoop review. Define the whole first. Then count equal parts or equal number-line intervals. This guide is printable; open the self-check answers to print the answer key.

sections.title: 7-1 Equal parts
text: Partition means divide into parts. Fraction parts of one shape must have equal area. Different cuts can make valid equal shares.

examples.title: A fair share
text: A strip has four equal-area pieces. Each piece is one fourth. Four uneven pieces would not be fourths.

steps.text: The complete outside shape is one whole.
Count 4 parts in ONE whole. This gives denominator 4.
A strip has four equal-area pieces. Each piece is one fourth. Four uneven pieces would not be fourths.

mistakes.mistake: Counting pieces without checking their sizes.
mistakes.fix: Check that all pieces have equal area.

checks.question: A sheet has three pieces: two small and one large. Are they thirds?
checks.answer: No. Thirds must have equal area.

sections.title: 7-2 Name the fraction
text: The denominator counts equal parts in ONE whole. The numerator counts the parts being described. A unit fraction has numerator 1.

examples.title: Selected pieces
text: This circle has six equal parts. Five are selected, so its selected fraction is 5/6.

steps.text: The complete outside shape is one whole.
Count 6 parts in ONE whole. This gives denominator 6.

mistakes.fix: Put the selected count on top and the number of parts in one whole below.

checks.question: Two of eight equal pieces are selected. What fraction is selected?
checks.answer: 2/8. The numerator is 2 and the denominator is 8.

sections.title: 7-3 Fractions on a number line
text: Find 0 and 1. Count the equal intervals between them, not the tick marks. Count from zero to the point to find the numerator.

examples.title: A point between zero and one
text: Four intervals fill one whole. The point is three intervals from zero, so it is 3/4.

steps.text: Start with 0 to 1: this interval is one whole.
Count 4 spaces between 0 and 1. The denominator is 4; ignore extra units for this count.
Four intervals fill one whole. The point is three intervals from zero, so it is 3/4.

mistakes.mistake: Using the number of tick marks as the denominator.
mistakes.fix: Count the spaces between marks from 0 to 1.

checks.question: There are seven marks including 0 and 1, evenly spaced. What denominator describes the line?
checks.answer: 6, because the seven marks enclose six equal intervals.

sections.title: 7-4 One whole
text: When every part of one whole is used, the numerator equals the denominator: b/b is one whole.

examples.title: All thirds
text: All three thirds are selected. The fraction 3/3 names one complete whole.

steps.text: The complete outside shape is one whole.
Count 3 parts in ONE whole. This gives denominator 3.
All three thirds are selected. The fraction 3/3 names one complete whole.

mistakes.fix: Six sixth-size parts together fill one whole.

checks.question: How many wholes are eight eighths?
checks.answer: One whole. All eight equal parts of the whole are present.

sections.title: 7-5 Whole numbers as fractions
text: A denominator of 1 means each part is one whole. A whole number n can be written n/1.

examples.title: Three whole units
text: Each box is one whole unit. Three whole-size parts are 3/1.

steps.text: Each complete outside shape is one whole. Count complete outlines separately.
Count 1 part in ONE whole. This gives denominator 1.
Each box is one whole unit. Three whole-size parts are 3/1.

mistakes.fix: 1/3 is one small part; 3/1 is three whole-size parts.

checks.question: Write six wholes as a fraction using whole-size parts.

sections.title: 7-6 Beyond one
text: Keep the same interval size beyond 1. Count intervals from zero; the denominator stays the number of intervals in ONE whole. A numerator larger than the denominator represents more than one.

examples.title: Seven thirds
text: Each whole has three intervals. The point is seven intervals from zero, so it is 7/3. It lies between 2 and 3.

steps.text: Start with 0 to 1: this interval is one whole.
Count 3 spaces between 0 and 1. The denominator is 3; ignore extra units for this count.
Each whole has three intervals. The point is seven intervals from zero, so it is 7/3. It lies between 2 and 3.

mistakes.mistake: Using every interval across the entire line as the denominator.
mistakes.fix: Only count intervals in one whole to find the denominator.

checks.question: Each whole has four intervals. A point is five intervals from zero. What fraction is it, and is it greater than one?
checks.answer: 5/4. It is greater than one because four fourths fill one whole and one fourth remains.

checks.question: Is nine fourths less than or greater than three wholes?
checks.answer: Less than three wholes. Three wholes are twelve fourths; nine fourths stop before that.

sections.title: 7-7 A fraction of a set
text: State which objects form the entire set. When each object is counted equally, the denominator is the number of objects in the whole set. A single object is a unit fraction of that set.

examples.title: A set of ten
text: All ten objects form one whole set. One selected object is 1/10 of the set. Three selected objects would be 3/10.

steps.text: All 10 objects together make the whole set.
